[1362](https://docs.rs#1362)/// Wrapper type for imported statics.
[1363](https://docs.rs#1363)///
[1364](https://docs.rs#1364)/// This type is used whenever a `static` is imported from a JS module, for
[1365](https://docs.rs#1365)/// example this import:
[1366](https://docs.rs#1366)///
[1367](https://docs.rs#1367)/// ```ignore
[1368](https://docs.rs#1368)/// #[wasm_bindgen]
[1369](https://docs.rs#1369)/// extern "C" {
[1370](https://docs.rs#1370)///     static console: JsValue;
[1371](https://docs.rs#1371)/// }
[1372](https://docs.rs#1372)/// ```
[1373](https://docs.rs#1373)///
[1374](https://docs.rs#1374)/// will generate in Rust a value that looks like:
[1375](https://docs.rs#1375)///
[1376](https://docs.rs#1376)/// ```ignore
[1377](https://docs.rs#1377)/// static console: JsStatic<JsValue> = ...;
[1378](https://docs.rs#1378)/// ```
[1379](https://docs.rs#1379)///
[1380](https://docs.rs#1380)/// This type implements `Deref` to the inner type so it's typically used as if
[1381](https://docs.rs#1381)/// it were `&T`.
[1382](https://docs.rs#1382)#[cfg(feature = "std")]
[1383](https://docs.rs#1383)#[deprecated = "use with `#[wasm_bindgen(thread_local_v2)]` instead"]
[1384](https://docs.rs#1384)pub struct JsStatic<T: 'static> {
[1385](https://docs.rs#1385)    #[doc(hidden)]
[1386](https://docs.rs#1386)    pub __inner: &'static std::thread::LocalKey<T>,
[1387](https://docs.rs#1387)}
[1388](https://docs.rs#1388)
[1389](https://docs.rs#1389)#[cfg(feature = "std")]
[1390](https://docs.rs#1390)#[allow(deprecated)]
[1391](https://docs.rs#1391)#[cfg(not(target_feature = "atomics"))]
[1392](https://docs.rs#1392)impl<T: crate::convert::FromWasmAbi + 'static> Deref for JsStatic<T> {
[1393](https://docs.rs#1393)    type Target = T;
[1394](https://docs.rs#1394)    fn deref(&self) -> &T {
[1395](https://docs.rs#1395)        unsafe { self.__inner.with(|ptr| &*(ptr as *const T)) }
[1396](https://docs.rs#1396)    }
[1397](https://docs.rs#1397)}
[1398](https://docs.rs#1398)
[1399](https://docs.rs#1399)/// Wrapper type for imported statics.
[1400](https://docs.rs#1400)///
[1401](https://docs.rs#1401)/// This type is used whenever a `static` is imported from a JS module, for
[1402](https://docs.rs#1402)/// example this import:
[1403](https://docs.rs#1403)///
[1404](https://docs.rs#1404)/// ```ignore
[1405](https://docs.rs#1405)/// #[wasm_bindgen]
[1406](https://docs.rs#1406)/// extern "C" {
[1407](https://docs.rs#1407)///     #[wasm_bindgen(thread_local_v2)]
[1408](https://docs.rs#1408)///     static console: JsValue;
[1409](https://docs.rs#1409)/// }
[1410](https://docs.rs#1410)/// ```
[1411](https://docs.rs#1411)///
[1412](https://docs.rs#1412)/// will generate in Rust a value that looks like:
[1413](https://docs.rs#1413)///
[1414](https://docs.rs#1414)/// ```ignore
[1415](https://docs.rs#1415)/// static console: JsThreadLocal<JsValue> = ...;
[1416](https://docs.rs#1416)/// ```
[1417](https://docs.rs#1417)pub struct JsThreadLocal<T: 'static> {
[1418](https://docs.rs#1418)    #[doc(hidden)]
[1419](https://docs.rs#1419)    #[cfg(not(target_feature = "atomics"))]
[1420](https://docs.rs#1420)    pub __inner: &'static __rt::LazyCell<T>,
[1421](https://docs.rs#1421)    #[doc(hidden)]
[1422](https://docs.rs#1422)    #[cfg(target_feature = "atomics")]
[1423](https://docs.rs#1423)    pub __inner: fn() -> *const T,
[1424](https://docs.rs#1424)}
[1425](https://docs.rs#1425)
[1426](https://docs.rs#1426)impl<T> JsThreadLocal<T> {
[1427](https://docs.rs#1427)    pub fn with<F, R>(&'static self, f: F) -> R
[1428](https://docs.rs#1428)    where
[1429](https://docs.rs#1429)        F: FnOnce(&T) -> R,
[1430](https://docs.rs#1430)    {
[1431](https://docs.rs#1431)        #[cfg(not(target_feature = "atomics"))]
[1432](https://docs.rs#1432)        return f(self.__inner);
[1433](https://docs.rs#1433)        #[cfg(target_feature = "atomics")]
[1434](https://docs.rs#1434)        f(unsafe { &*(self.__inner)() })
[1435](https://docs.rs#1435)    }
[1436](https://docs.rs#1436)}
[1437](https://docs.rs#1437)
[1438](https://docs.rs#1438)#[cold]
[1439](https://docs.rs#1439)#[inline(never)]
[1440](https://docs.rs#1440)#[deprecated(note = "renamed to `throw_str`")]
[1441](https://docs.rs#1441)#[doc(hidden)]

[1443](https://docs.rs#1443)    throw_str(s)
[1444](https://docs.rs#1444)}
[1445](https://docs.rs#1445)
[1446](https://docs.rs#1446)/// Throws a JS exception.
[1447](https://docs.rs#1447)///
[1448](https://docs.rs#1448)/// This function will throw a JS exception with the message provided. The
[1449](https://docs.rs#1449)/// function will not return as the Wasm stack will be popped when the exception
[1450](https://docs.rs#1450)/// is thrown.
[1451](https://docs.rs#1451)///
[1452](https://docs.rs#1452)/// Note that it is very easy to leak memory with this function because this
[1453](https://docs.rs#1453)/// function, unlike `panic!` on other platforms, **will not run destructors**.
[1454](https://docs.rs#1454)/// It's recommended to return a `Result` where possible to avoid the worry of
[1455](https://docs.rs#1455)/// leaks.
[1456](https://docs.rs#1456)///
[1457](https://docs.rs#1457)/// If you need destructors to run, consider using `panic!` when building with
[1458](https://docs.rs#1458)/// `-Cpanic=unwind`. If the `std` feature is used panics will be caught at the
[1459](https://docs.rs#1459)/// JavaScript boundary and converted to JavaScript exceptions.
[1460](https://docs.rs#1460)#[cold]
[1461](https://docs.rs#1461)#[inline(never)]
[1462](https://docs.rs#1462)pub fn throw_str(s: &str) -> ! {
[1463](https://docs.rs#1463)    __wbindgen_throw(s);
[1464](https://docs.rs#1464)    unsafe { core::hint::unreachable_unchecked() }
[1465](https://docs.rs#1465)}
[1466](https://docs.rs#1466)
[1467](https://docs.rs#1467)/// Rethrow a JS exception
[1468](https://docs.rs#1468)///
[1469](https://docs.rs#1469)/// This function will throw a JS exception with the JS value provided. This
[1470](https://docs.rs#1470)/// function will not return and the Wasm stack will be popped until the point
[1471](https://docs.rs#1471)/// of entry of Wasm itself.
[1472](https://docs.rs#1472)///
[1473](https://docs.rs#1473)/// Note that it is very easy to leak memory with this function because this
[1474](https://docs.rs#1474)/// function, unlike `panic!` on other platforms, **will not run destructors**.
[1475](https://docs.rs#1475)/// It's recommended to return a `Result` where possible to avoid the worry of
[1476](https://docs.rs#1476)/// leaks.
[1477](https://docs.rs#1477)///
[1478](https://docs.rs#1478)/// If you need destructors to run, consider using `panic!` when building with
[1479](https://docs.rs#1479)/// `-Cpanic=unwind`. If the `std` feature is used panics will be caught at the
[1480](https://docs.rs#1480)/// JavaScript boundary and converted to JavaScript exceptions.
[1481](https://docs.rs#1481)#[cold]
[1482](https://docs.rs#1482)#[inline(never)]
[1483](https://docs.rs#1483)pub fn throw_val(s: JsValue) -> ! {
[1484](https://docs.rs#1484)    __wbindgen_rethrow(s);
[1485](https://docs.rs#1485)    unsafe { core::hint::unreachable_unchecked() }
[1486](https://docs.rs#1486)}
[1487](https://docs.rs#1487)
[1488](https://docs.rs#1488)/// Get the count of live `externref`s / `JsValue`s in `wasm-bindgen`'s heap.
[1489](https://docs.rs#1489)///
[1490](https://docs.rs#1490)/// ## Usage
[1491](https://docs.rs#1491)///
[1492](https://docs.rs#1492)/// This is intended for debugging and writing tests.
[1493](https://docs.rs#1493)///
[1494](https://docs.rs#1494)/// To write a test that asserts against unnecessarily keeping `anref`s /
[1495](https://docs.rs#1495)/// `JsValue`s alive:
[1496](https://docs.rs#1496)///
[1497](https://docs.rs#1497)/// * get an initial live count,
[1498](https://docs.rs#1498)///
[1499](https://docs.rs#1499)/// * perform some series of operations or function calls that should clean up
[1500](https://docs.rs#1500)///   after themselves, and should not keep holding onto `externref`s / `JsValue`s
[1501](https://docs.rs#1501)///   after completion,
[1502](https://docs.rs#1502)///
[1503](https://docs.rs#1503)/// * get the final live count,
[1504](https://docs.rs#1504)///
[1505](https://docs.rs#1505)/// * and assert that the initial and final counts are the same.
[1506](https://docs.rs#1506)///
[1507](https://docs.rs#1507)/// ## What is Counted
[1508](https://docs.rs#1508)///
[1509](https://docs.rs#1509)/// Note that this only counts the *owned* `externref`s / `JsValue`s that end up in
[1510](https://docs.rs#1510)/// `wasm-bindgen`'s heap. It does not count borrowed `externref`s / `JsValue`s
[1511](https://docs.rs#1511)/// that are on its stack.
[1512](https://docs.rs#1512)///
[1513](https://docs.rs#1513)/// For example, these `JsValue`s are accounted for:
[1514](https://docs.rs#1514)///
[1515](https://docs.rs#1515)/// ```ignore
[1516](https://docs.rs#1516)/// #[wasm_bindgen]
[1517](https://docs.rs#1517)/// pub fn my_function(this_is_counted: JsValue) {
[1518](https://docs.rs#1518)///     let also_counted = JsValue::from_str("hi");
[1519](https://docs.rs#1519)///     assert!(wasm_bindgen::externref_heap_live_count() >= 2);
[1520](https://docs.rs#1520)/// }
[1521](https://docs.rs#1521)/// ```
[1522](https://docs.rs#1522)///
[1523](https://docs.rs#1523)/// While this borrowed `JsValue` ends up on the stack, not the heap, and
[1524](https://docs.rs#1524)/// therefore is not accounted for:
[1525](https://docs.rs#1525)///
[1526](https://docs.rs#1526)/// ```ignore
[1527](https://docs.rs#1527)/// #[wasm_bindgen]
[1528](https://docs.rs#1528)/// pub fn my_other_function(this_is_not_counted: &JsValue) {
[1529](https://docs.rs#1529)///     // ...
[1530](https://docs.rs#1530)/// }
[1531](https://docs.rs#1531)/// ```
[1532](https://docs.rs#1532)pub fn externref_heap_live_count() -> u32 {
[1533](https://docs.rs#1533)    __wbindgen_externref_heap_live_count()
[1534](https://docs.rs#1534)}
[1535](https://docs.rs#1535)
[1536](https://docs.rs#1536)#[doc(hidden)]
[1537](https://docs.rs#1537)pub fn anyref_heap_live_count() -> u32 {
[1538](https://docs.rs#1538)    externref_heap_live_count()
[1539](https://docs.rs#1539)}
[1540](https://docs.rs#1540)
[1541](https://docs.rs#1541)/// An extension trait for `Option<T>` and `Result<T, E>` for unwrapping the `T`
[1542](https://docs.rs#1542)/// value, or throwing a JS error if it is not available.
[1543](https://docs.rs#1543)///
[1544](https://docs.rs#1544)/// These methods should have a smaller code size footprint than the normal
[1545](https://docs.rs#1545)/// `Option::unwrap` and `Option::expect` methods, but they are specific to
[1546](https://docs.rs#1546)/// working with Wasm and JS.
[1547](https://docs.rs#1547)///
[1548](https://docs.rs#1548)/// On non-wasm32 targets, defaults to the normal unwrap/expect calls.
[1549](https://docs.rs#1549)///
[1550](https://docs.rs#1550)/// # Example
[1551](https://docs.rs#1551)///
[1552](https://docs.rs#1552)/// ```
[1553](https://docs.rs#1553)/// use wasm_bindgen::prelude::*;
[1554](https://docs.rs#1554)///
[1555](https://docs.rs#1555)/// // If the value is `Option::Some` or `Result::Ok`, then we just get the
[1556](https://docs.rs#1556)/// // contained `T` value.
[1557](https://docs.rs#1557)/// let x = Some(42);
[1558](https://docs.rs#1558)/// assert_eq!(x.unwrap_throw(), 42);
[1559](https://docs.rs#1559)///
[1560](https://docs.rs#1560)/// let y: Option<i32> = None;
[1561](https://docs.rs#1561)///
[1562](https://docs.rs#1562)/// // This call would throw an error to JS!
[1563](https://docs.rs#1563)/// //
[1564](https://docs.rs#1564)/// //     y.unwrap_throw()
[1565](https://docs.rs#1565)/// //
[1566](https://docs.rs#1566)/// // And this call would throw an error to JS with a custom error message!
[1567](https://docs.rs#1567)/// //
[1568](https://docs.rs#1568)/// //     y.expect_throw("woopsie daisy!")
[1569](https://docs.rs#1569)/// ```
[1570](https://docs.rs#1570)pub trait UnwrapThrowExt<T>: Sized {
[1571](https://docs.rs#1571)    /// Unwrap this `Option` or `Result`, but instead of panicking on failure,
[1572](https://docs.rs#1572)    /// throw an exception to JavaScript.
[1573](https://docs.rs#1573)    #[cfg_attr(
[1574](https://docs.rs#1574)        any(
[1575](https://docs.rs#1575)            debug_assertions,
[1576](https://docs.rs#1576)            not(all(target_family = "wasm", not(target_os = "wasi")))
[1577](https://docs.rs#1577)        ),
[1578](https://docs.rs#1578)        track_caller
[1579](https://docs.rs#1579)    )]
[1580](https://docs.rs#1580)    fn unwrap_throw(self) -> T {
[1581](https://docs.rs#1581)        if cfg!(all(
[1582](https://docs.rs#1582)            debug_assertions,
[1583](https://docs.rs#1583)            all(target_family = "wasm", not(target_os = "wasi"))
[1584](https://docs.rs#1584)        )) {
[1585](https://docs.rs#1585)            let loc = core::panic::Location::caller();
[1586](https://docs.rs#1586)            let msg = alloc::format!(
[1587](https://docs.rs#1587)                "called `{}::unwrap_throw()` ({}:{}:{})",
[1588](https://docs.rs#1588)                core::any::type_name::<Self>(),
[1589](https://docs.rs#1589)                loc.file(),
[1590](https://docs.rs#1590)                loc.line(),
[1591](https://docs.rs#1591)                loc.column()
[1592](https://docs.rs#1592)            );
[1593](https://docs.rs#1593)            self.expect_throw(&msg)
[1594](https://docs.rs#1594)        } else {
[1595](https://docs.rs#1595)            self.expect_throw("called `unwrap_throw()`")
[1596](https://docs.rs#1596)        }
[1597](https://docs.rs#1597)    }
[1598](https://docs.rs#1598)
[1599](https://docs.rs#1599)    /// Unwrap this container's `T` value, or throw an error to JS with the
[1600](https://docs.rs#1600)    /// given message if the `T` value is unavailable (e.g. an `Option<T>` is
[1601](https://docs.rs#1601)    /// `None`).
[1602](https://docs.rs#1602)    #[cfg_attr(
[1603](https://docs.rs#1603)        any(
[1604](https://docs.rs#1604)            debug_assertions,
[1605](https://docs.rs#1605)            not(all(target_family = "wasm", not(target_os = "wasi")))
[1606](https://docs.rs#1606)        ),
[1607](https://docs.rs#1607)        track_caller
[1608](https://docs.rs#1608)    )]
[1609](https://docs.rs#1609)    fn expect_throw(self, message: &str) -> T;
[1610](https://docs.rs#1610)}
[1611](https://docs.rs#1611)
[1612](https://docs.rs#1612)impl<T> UnwrapThrowExt<T> for Option<T> {
[1613](https://docs.rs#1613)    fn unwrap_throw(self) -> T {
[1614](https://docs.rs#1614)        const MSG: &str = "called `Option::unwrap_throw()` on a `None` value";
[1615](https://docs.rs#1615)
[1616](https://docs.rs#1616)        if cfg!(all(target_family = "wasm", not(target_os = "wasi"))) {
[1617](https://docs.rs#1617)            if let Some(val) = self {
[1618](https://docs.rs#1618)                val
[1619](https://docs.rs#1619)            } else if cfg!(debug_assertions) {
[1620](https://docs.rs#1620)                let loc = core::panic::Location::caller();
[1621](https://docs.rs#1621)                let msg = alloc::format!("{MSG} ({}:{}:{})", loc.file(), loc.line(), loc.column(),);
[1622](https://docs.rs#1622)
[1623](https://docs.rs#1623)                throw_str(&msg)
[1624](https://docs.rs#1624)            } else {
[1625](https://docs.rs#1625)                throw_str(MSG)
[1626](https://docs.rs#1626)            }
[1627](https://docs.rs#1627)        } else {
[1628](https://docs.rs#1628)            self.expect(MSG)
[1629](https://docs.rs#1629)        }
[1630](https://docs.rs#1630)    }
[1631](https://docs.rs#1631)
[1632](https://docs.rs#1632)    fn expect_throw(self, message: &str) -> T {
[1633](https://docs.rs#1633)        if cfg!(all(target_family = "wasm", not(target_os = "wasi"))) {
[1634](https://docs.rs#1634)            if let Some(val) = self {
[1635](https://docs.rs#1635)                val
[1636](https://docs.rs#1636)            } else if cfg!(debug_assertions) {
[1637](https://docs.rs#1637)                let loc = core::panic::Location::caller();
[1638](https://docs.rs#1638)                let msg =
[1639](https://docs.rs#1639)                    alloc::format!("{message} ({}:{}:{})", loc.file(), loc.line(), loc.column(),);
[1640](https://docs.rs#1640)
[1641](https://docs.rs#1641)                throw_str(&msg)
[1642](https://docs.rs#1642)            } else {
[1643](https://docs.rs#1643)                throw_str(message)
[1644](https://docs.rs#1644)            }
[1645](https://docs.rs#1645)        } else {
[1646](https://docs.rs#1646)            self.expect(message)
[1647](https://docs.rs#1647)        }
[1648](https://docs.rs#1648)    }
[1649](https://docs.rs#1649)}

[1651](https://docs.rs#1651)impl<T, E> UnwrapThrowExt<T> for Result<T, E>

[1653](https://docs.rs#1653)    E: core::fmt::Debug,
[1654](https://docs.rs#1654){
[1655](https://docs.rs#1655)    fn unwrap_throw(self) -> T {
[1656](https://docs.rs#1656)        const MSG: &str = "called `Result::unwrap_throw()` on an `Err` value";
[1657](https://docs.rs#1657)
[1658](https://docs.rs#1658)        if cfg!(all(target_family = "wasm", not(target_os = "wasi"))) {
[1659](https://docs.rs#1659)            match self {
[1660](https://docs.rs#1660)                Ok(val) => val,
[1661](https://docs.rs#1661)                Err(err) => {
[1662](https://docs.rs#1662)                    if cfg!(debug_assertions) {
[1663](https://docs.rs#1663)                        let loc = core::panic::Location::caller();
[1664](https://docs.rs#1664)                        let msg = alloc::format!(
[1665](https://docs.rs#1665)                            "{MSG} ({}:{}:{}): {err:?}",
[1666](https://docs.rs#1666)                            loc.file(),
[1667](https://docs.rs#1667)                            loc.line(),
[1668](https://docs.rs#1668)                            loc.column(),
[1669](https://docs.rs#1669)                        );
[1670](https://docs.rs#1670)
[1671](https://docs.rs#1671)                        throw_str(&msg)
[1672](https://docs.rs#1672)                    } else {
[1673](https://docs.rs#1673)                        throw_str(MSG)
[1674](https://docs.rs#1674)                    }
[1675](https://docs.rs#1675)                }
[1676](https://docs.rs#1676)            }
[1677](https://docs.rs#1677)        } else {
[1678](https://docs.rs#1678)            self.expect(MSG)
[1679](https://docs.rs#1679)        }
[1680](https://docs.rs#1680)    }
[1681](https://docs.rs#1681)
[1682](https://docs.rs#1682)    fn expect_throw(self, message: &str) -> T {
[1683](https://docs.rs#1683)        if cfg!(all(target_family = "wasm", not(target_os = "wasi"))) {

[1685](https://docs.rs#1685)                Ok(val) => val,
[1686](https://docs.rs#1686)                Err(err) => {
[1687](https://docs.rs#1687)                    if cfg!(debug_assertions) {
[1688](https://docs.rs#1688)                        let loc = core::panic::Location::caller();
[1689](https://docs.rs#1689)                        let msg = alloc::format!(
[1690](https://docs.rs#1690)                            "{message} ({}:{}:{}): {err:?}",
[1691](https://docs.rs#1691)                            loc.file(),
[1692](https://docs.rs#1692)                            loc.line(),

[1694](https://docs.rs#1694)                        );
[1695](https://docs.rs#1695)
[1696](https://docs.rs#1696)                        throw_str(&msg)

[1741](https://docs.rs#1741)/// A wrapper type around slices and vectors for binding the `Uint8ClampedArray`

[1745](https://docs.rs#1745)/// then you can define it as taking one of these types:
[1746](https://docs.rs#1746)///
[1747](https://docs.rs#1747)/// * `Clamped<&[u8]>`
[1748](https://docs.rs#1748)/// * `Clamped<&mut [u8]>`
[1749](https://docs.rs#1749)/// * `Clamped<Vec<u8>>`
[1750](https://docs.rs#1750)///
[1751](https://docs.rs#1751)/// All of these types will show up as `Uint8ClampedArray` in JS and will have
[1752](https://docs.rs#1752)/// different forms of ownership in Rust.
[1753](https://docs.rs#1753)#[derive(Copy, Clone, PartialEq, Debug, Eq)]

[1760](https://docs.rs#1760)        &self.0
[1761](https://docs.rs#1761)    }
[1762](https://docs.rs#1762)}
[1763](https://docs.rs#1763)

[1769](https://docs.rs#1769)
[1770](https://docs.rs#1770)/// Convenience type for use on exported `fn() -> Result<T, JsError>` functions, where you wish to
[1771](https://docs.rs#1771)/// throw a JavaScript `Error` object.
[1772](https://docs.rs#1772)///
[1773](https://docs.rs#1773)/// You can get wasm_bindgen to throw basic errors by simply returning
[1774](https://docs.rs#1774)/// `Err(JsError::new("message"))` from such a function.
[1775](https://docs.rs#1775)///
[1776](https://docs.rs#1776)/// For more complex error handling, `JsError` implements `From<T> where T: std::error::Error` by
[1777](https://docs.rs#1777)/// converting it to a string, so you can use it with `?`. Many Rust error types already do this,
[1778](https://docs.rs#1778)/// and you can use [`thiserror`](https://crates.io/crates/thiserror) to derive Display
[1779](https://docs.rs#1779)/// implementations easily or use any number of boxed error types that implement it already.
[1780](https://docs.rs#1780)///
[1781](https://docs.rs#1781)///
[1782](https://docs.rs#1782)/// To allow JavaScript code to catch only your errors, you may wish to add a subclass of `Error`
[1783](https://docs.rs#1783)/// in a JS module, and then implement `Into<JsValue>` directly on a type and instantiate that
[1784](https://docs.rs#1784)/// subclass. In that case, you would not need `JsError` at all.
[1785](https://docs.rs#1785)///
[1786](https://docs.rs#1786)/// ### Basic example
[1787](https://docs.rs#1787)///
[1788](https://docs.rs#1788)/// ```rust,no_run
[1789](https://docs.rs#1789)/// use wasm_bindgen::prelude::*;
[1790](https://docs.rs#1790)///
[1791](https://docs.rs#1791)/// #[wasm_bindgen]
[1792](https://docs.rs#1792)/// pub fn throwing_function() -> Result<(), JsError> {

# IntoJsGeneric in wasm_bindgen::convert - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/wasm_bindgen/convert/trait.IntoJsGeneric.html

```
pub trait IntoJsGeneric {
    type
```
[JsCanon](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.JsCanon): [JsGeneric](https://docs.rs/trait.JsGeneric.html);
    // Required method
    fn [to_js](https://docs.rs#tymethod.to_js)(self) -> Self::[JsCanon](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoJsGeneric.html#associatedtype.JsCanon);
}## Expand description

Value conversion from a type into its canonical [ JsGeneric](https://docs.rs/trait.JsGeneric.html) form.

This trait allows types to be converted into JsGeneric supported types, which are required to be erasably generic with JsValue.

The single associated type — rather than a free type parameter bounded by
`AsRef<T>` — is what makes collection-style APIs infer annotation-free.
Given an input `A`, there is exactly one `A::JsCanon`, so rustc never has
to search across multiple `AsRef` impls to pick a target element type.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementations-1)Implementations

Provided impls:

- `JsValue`
- Every `#[wasm_bindgen]`-imported type (identity — emitted by the macro).
- Every generic `js_sys`container (`Array<T>`,`Promise<T>`,`Set<T>`, …) provides its own identity impl owned by`js_sys`.
- References to cloneable implementors, so borrowed iteration can still produce owned JS-generic values.

This trait is deliberately *not* blanket-implemented over all [ JsGeneric](https://docs.rs/trait.JsGeneric.html)
types: each implementor explicitly opts in, which leaves room for future
wrapper types to pick a non-identity

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoJsGeneric.html#associatedtype.JsCanon)

`Self::JsCanon`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# JsGeneric in wasm_bindgen::convert - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/wasm_bindgen/convert/trait.JsGeneric.html

```
pub trait JsGeneric:

```
[ErasableGeneric](https://docs.rs/trait.ErasableGeneric.html)<Repr = [JsValue](https://docs.rs/struct.JsValue.html)>
    + [UpcastFrom](https://docs.rs/trait.UpcastFrom.html)<Self>
    + [Upcast](https://docs.rs/trait.Upcast.html)<Self>
    + [Upcast](https://docs.rs/trait.Upcast.html)<[JsValue](https://docs.rs/struct.JsValue.html)>
    + [JsCast](https://docs.rs/trait.JsCast.html)
    + 'static { }## Expand description

A convenience trait for types that erase to [ JsValue](https://docs.rs/struct.JsValue.html).

This is a shorthand for `ErasableGeneric<Repr = JsValue>`, used as a bound
on generic parameters that must be representable as JavaScript values.

[§](https://docs.rs#when-to-use)When to Use

Use `JsGeneric` as a trait bound when you need a generic type that:

- Can be passed to/from JavaScript
- Is type-erased to `JsValue`at the FFI boundary

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use wasm_bindgen::JsGeneric;
fn process_js_values<T: JsGeneric>(items: &[T]) {
    // T can be any JS-compatible type
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#implementors-1)Implementors

This trait is automatically implemented for all types that implement
`ErasableGeneric<Repr = JsValue>`, including:

- All `js_sys`types (`Object`,`Array`,`Function`, etc.)
- `JsValue`itself
- Custom types imported via `#[wasm_bindgen]`

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# wasm_bindgen::closure - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/wasm_bindgen/closure/index.html

## Expand description

Support for closures in `wasm-bindgen`

This module defines the [ ScopedClosure](https://docs.rs/struct.ScopedClosure.html) type which is used to pass Rust closures
to JavaScript. All closures are unwind safe by default: panics are caught and converted to
JavaScript exceptions when built with

`panic=unwind`.[§](https://docs.rs#immutable-by-default)Immutable by Default

The closure API defaults to **immutable** (`Fn`) closures because they are more
likely to satisfy `UnwindSafe` automatically:

- `&T`where- `T: RefUnwindSafe`is- `UnwindSafe`
- `&mut T`is- **never**- `UnwindSafe`regardless of- `T`

This means:

- `ScopedClosure::borrow`- `Fn`closure
- `ScopedClosure::borrow_mut`- `FnMut`closure

Immutable closures can be upcasted to mutable closures using [ upcast_ref](crate::Upcast::upcast_ref).

[§](https://docs.rs#type-aliases)Type Aliases

- `ScopedClosure<'a, T>`
- `Closure<T>`- `ScopedClosure<'static, T>`(for backwards compatibility)

[§](https://docs.rs#unwind-safety)Unwind Safety

For immediate/synchronous callbacks, use `&dyn FnMut` / `&dyn Fn`, when you are
**absolutely sure** the code will support unwind safety.

For [ ScopedClosure](https://docs.rs/struct.ScopedClosure.html), the default constructors (

`borrow`, `borrow_mut`, `own`) catch
panics, while the `_aborting` variants (`borrow_aborting`, `borrow_mut_aborting`, etc.) do not.[§](https://docs.rs#ownership-model)Ownership Model

`ScopedClosure` follows the same ownership model as other wasm-bindgen types:
the JavaScript reference remains valid until the Rust value is dropped. When
dropped, the closure is invalidated and any subsequent calls from JavaScript
will throw an exception.

For borrowed closures created with `borrow`/`borrow_mut`, Rust’s borrow checker
ensures the `ScopedClosure` cannot outlive the closure’s captured data.

See the [ ScopedClosure](https://docs.rs/struct.ScopedClosure.html) type documentation for detailed examples.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Scoped](https://docs.rs/struct.ScopedClosure.html)- Closure
- A closure with a lifetime parameter that represents a Rust closure passed to JavaScript.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Closure](https://docs.rs/type.Closure.html)
- Alias for `ScopedClosure<'static, T>`

---

# link_to in wasm_bindgen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/wasm_bindgen/macro.link_to.html

`link_to!() { /* proc-macro */ }`## Expand description

This macro takes a JS module as input and returns a URL that can be used to access it at runtime.

The module can be specified in a few ways:

- You can use `inline_js = "..."`to create an inline JS file.
- You can use `module = "/foo/bar"`to reference a file relative to the root of the crate the macro is invoked in.

The returned URL can be used for things like creating workers/worklets:

```
use web_sys::Worker;
let worker = Worker::new(&wasm_bindgen::link_to!(module = "/src/worker.js"));
```

---

# JsError in wasm_bindgen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsError.html

`pub struct JsError { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Convenience type for use on exported `fn() -> Result<T, JsError>` functions, where you wish to
throw a JavaScript `Error` object.

You can get wasm_bindgen to throw basic errors by simply returning
`Err(JsError::new("message"))` from such a function.

For more complex error handling, `JsError` implements `From<T> where T: std::error::Error` by
converting it to a string, so you can use it with `?`. Many Rust error types already do this,
and you can use [ thiserror](https://crates.io/crates/thiserror) to derive Display
implementations easily or use any number of boxed error types that implement it already.

To allow JavaScript code to catch only your errors, you may wish to add a subclass of `Error`
in a JS module, and then implement `Into<JsValue>` directly on a type and instantiate that
subclass. In that case, you would not need `JsError` at all.

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-example)Basic example

```
use wasm_bindgen::prelude::*;
#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn throwing_function() -> Result<(), JsError> {
    Err(JsError::new("message"))
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#complex-example)Complex Example

```
use wasm_bindgen::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
enum MyErrorType {
    SomeError,
}
use core::fmt;
impl std::error::Error for MyErrorType {}
impl fmt::Display for MyErrorType {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "display implementation becomes the error message")
    }
}
fn internal_api() -> Result<(), MyErrorType> {
    Err(MyErrorType::SomeError)
}
#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn throwing_function() -> Result<(), JsError> {
    internal_api()?;
    Ok(())
}
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# JsStatic in wasm_bindgen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsStatic.html

# Struct JsStatic

[Source](../src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#1384-1387) `pub struct JsStatic<T: 'static> {  }`

👎Deprecated: use with `#[wasm_bindgen(thread_local_v2)]` instead

 ## Expand description

Wrapper type for imported statics.

This type is used whenever a `static` is imported from a JS module, for
example this import:

[ⓘ](#)```
#[wasm_bindgen]
extern "C" {
    static console: JsValue;
}
```

will generate in Rust a value that looks like:

[ⓘ](#)`static console: JsStatic<JsValue> = ...;`

This type implements `Deref` to the inner type so it’s typically used as if
it were `&T`.

[Source](../src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#1392-1397)[§](#impl-Deref-for-JsStatic%3CT%3E)Available on **crate feature **`std` and non-target feature `atomics` only.

The resulting type after dereferencing.

Dereferences the value.

Immutably borrows from an owned value.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html#tymethod.borrow)

Mutably borrows from an owned value.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.BorrowMut.html#tymethod.borrow_mut)

Returns the argument unchanged.

Calls `U::from(self)`.

That is, this conversion is whatever the implementation of
[From](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)<T> for U

🔬This is a nightly-only experimental API. (`arbitrary_self_types`)

The target type on which the method may be called.

The type returned in the event of a conversion error.

Performs the conversion.

The type returned in the event of a conversion error.

Performs the conversion.

Perform a zero-cost type-safe upcast to a wider ref type within the Wasm
bindgen generics type system.

[Read more](convert/trait.Upcast.html#method.upcast)

Perform a zero-cost type-safe upcast to a wider type within the Wasm
bindgen generics type system.

[Read more](convert/trait.Upcast.html#method.upcast_into)

# JsValue in wasm_bindgen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/wasm_bindgen/struct.JsValue.html

`pub struct JsValue { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Representation of an object owned by JS.

A `JsValue` doesn’t actually live in Rust right now but actually in a table
owned by the `wasm-bindgen` generated JS glue code. Eventually the ownership
will transfer into Wasm directly and this will likely become more efficient,
but for now it may be slightly slow.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Creates a new JS value which is a string.

The utf-8 string provided is copied to the JS heap and the string will be owned by the JS garbage collector.

Creates a new JS value which is a number.

This function creates a JS value representing a number (a heap allocated number) and returns a handle to the JS version of it.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#231-233)#### pub fn [bigint_from_str](https://docs.rs#method.bigint_from_str)(s: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [JsValue](https://docs.rs/struct.JsValue.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#231-233)

#### pub fn [bigint_from_str](https://docs.rs#method.bigint_from_str)(s: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [JsValue](https://docs.rs/struct.JsValue.html)

Creates a new JS value which is a bigint from a string representing a number.

This function creates a JS value representing a bigint (a heap allocated large integer) and returns a handle to the JS version of it.

Creates a new JS value which is a boolean.

This function creates a JS object representing a boolean (a heap allocated boolean) and returns a handle to the JS version of it.

Creates a new JS symbol with the optional description specified.

This function will invoke the `Symbol` constructor in JS and return the
JS object corresponding to the symbol created.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#293-299)#### pub fn [from_serde](https://docs.rs#method.from_serde)<T>(t: [&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0.150/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_json/error/type.Result.html)<[JsValue](https://docs.rs/struct.JsValue.html)>

causes dependency cycles, use `serde-wasm-bindgen` or `gloo_utils::format::JsValueSerdeExt` instead

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#293-299)

#### pub fn [from_serde](https://docs.rs#method.from_serde)<T>(t: [&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0.150/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_json/error/type.Result.html)<[JsValue](https://docs.rs/struct.JsValue.html)>

causes dependency cycles, use `serde-wasm-bindgen` or `gloo_utils::format::JsValueSerdeExt` instead

Creates a new `JsValue` from the JSON serialization of the object `t`
provided.

**This function is deprecated**, due to [creating a dependency cycle in
some circumstances](https://github.com/wasm-bindgen/wasm-bindgen/issues/2770). Use [ serde-wasm-bindgen](https://docs.rs/serde-wasm-bindgen) or

[instead.](https://docs.rs/gloo-utils/latest/gloo_utils/format/trait.JsValueSerdeExt.html)

`gloo_utils::format::JsValueSerdeExt`This function will serialize the provided value `t` to a JSON string,
send the JSON string to JS, parse it into a JS object, and then return
a handle to the JS object. This is unlikely to be super speedy so it’s
not recommended for large payloads, but it’s a nice to have in some
situations!

Usage of this API requires activating the `serde-serialize` feature of
the `wasm-bindgen` crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

Returns any error encountered when serializing `T` into JSON.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#324-333)#### pub fn [into_serde](https://docs.rs#method.into_serde)<T>(&self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0.150/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_json/error/type.Result.html)<T>

causes dependency cycles, use `serde-wasm-bindgen` or `gloo_utils::format::JsValueSerdeExt` instead

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasm_bindgen/lib.rs.html#324-333)

#### pub fn [into_serde](https://docs.rs#method.into_serde)<T>(&self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0.150/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_json/error/type.Result.html)<T>

causes dependency cycles, use `serde-wasm-bindgen` or `gloo_utils::format::JsValueSerdeExt` instead

Invokes `JSON.stringify` on this value and then parses the resulting
JSON into an arbitrary Rust value.

**This function is deprecated**, due to [creating a dependency cycle in
some circumstances](https://github.com/wasm-bindgen/wasm-bindgen/issues/2770). Use [ serde-wasm-bindgen](https://docs.rs/serde-wasm-bindgen) or

[instead.](https://docs.rs/gloo-utils/latest/gloo_utils/format/trait.JsValueSerdeExt.html)

`gloo_utils::format::JsValueSerdeExt`This function will first call `JSON.stringify` on the `JsValue` itself.
The resulting string is then passed into Rust which then parses it as
JSON into the resulting value.

Usage of this API requires activating the `serde-serialize` feature of
the `wasm-bindgen` crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-1)Errors

Returns any error encountered when parsing the JSON into a `T`.

Returns the `f64` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
number.

If this JS value is not an instance of a number then this returns
`None`.

If this JS value is a string value, this function copies the JS string
value into Wasm linear memory, encoded as UTF-8, and returns it as a
Rust `String`.

To avoid the copying and re-encoding, consider the
`JsString::try_from()` function from [js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys)
instead.

If this JS value is not an instance of a string or if it’s not valid
utf-8 then this returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#utf-16-vs-utf-8)UTF-16 vs UTF-8

JavaScript strings in general are encoded as UTF-16, but Rust strings
are encoded as UTF-8. This can cause the Rust string to look a bit
different than the JS string sometimes. For more details see the
[documentation about the  str type](https://wasm-bindgen.github.io/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/str.html) which contains a few
caveats about the encodings.

Returns the `bool` value of this JS value if it’s an instance of a
boolean.

If this JS value is not an instance of a boolean then this returns
`None`.

# Parent in wasm_bindgen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/wasm_bindgen/struct.Parent.html

`pub struct Parent<T> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Storage wrapper for the auto-injected `parent` field on a struct that
declares `#[wasm_bindgen(extends = Parent)]`.

Under the hood this is an `Rc<WasmRefCell<T>>` so that wasm-bindgen can
produce a separately-refcounted parent pointer for JS-side prototype
dispatch. Use [ Parent::borrow](https://docs.rs/struct.Parent.html#method.borrow) /

[to access the inner value. You should not need to construct](https://docs.rs/struct.Parent.html#method.borrow_mut)

`Parent::borrow_mut``Parent<T>` directly
outside the child’s constructor; the [impl is the typical way to initialize the injected](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From<T>``parent` field.`Clone` is a cheap `Rc` clone — both copies point at the same parent
data. `Debug` prints the wrapper plus the inner `T` (when `T: Debug`).

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# ErasableGeneric in wasm_bindgen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/wasm_bindgen/trait.ErasableGeneric.html

```
pub unsafe trait ErasableGeneric {
    type
```
[Repr](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Repr): 'static;
}## Expand description

Private marker trait for erasable generics - types with this trait have the same repr for all generic param values, and can therefore be transmuted on the singular Repr type representation on ABI boundaries.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

This type must only be implemented on types known to be repr equivalent to their Repr type.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

[instanceof](https://docs.rs#tymethod.instanceof)(val: &[JsValue](https://docs.rs/struct.JsValue.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html);

    // Provided methods
    fn [has_type](https://docs.rs#method.has_type)<T>(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)
       where T: [JsCast](https://docs.rs/trait.JsCast.html) { ... }
[dyn_into](https://docs.rs#method.dyn_into)<T>(self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, Self>
       where T: [JsCast](https://docs.rs/trait.JsCast.html) { ... }
[dyn_ref](https://docs.rs#method.dyn_ref)<T>(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)>
       where T: [JsCast](https://docs.rs/trait.JsCast.html) { ... }
[unchecked_into](https://docs.rs#method.unchecked_into)<T>(self) -> T
       where T: [JsCast](https://docs.rs/trait.JsCast.html) { ... }
[unchecked_ref](https://docs.rs#method.unchecked_ref)<T>(&self) -> [&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)
       where T: [JsCast](https://docs.rs/trait.JsCast.html) { ... }
[is_instance_of](https://docs.rs#method.is_instance_of)<T>(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)
       where T: [JsCast](https://docs.rs/trait.JsCast.html) { ... }
[is_type_of](https://docs.rs#method.is_type_of)(val: &[JsValue](https://docs.rs/struct.JsValue.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html) { ... }
}## Expand description

A trait for dynamic checked and unchecked casting between JS types.

Unlike [`crate::Upcast`], which provides type-safe zero-cost type
conversions for generic type wrappers, this trait can be used to
perform arbitrary casts with JS instance checking.

Specified [in an RFC](https://github.com/rustwasm/rfcs/blob/master/text/002-wasm-bindgen-inheritance-casting.md) this trait is intended to provide support for
casting JS values between different types of one another. In JS there aren’t
many static types but we’ve ascribed JS values with static types in Rust,
yet they often need to be switched to other types temporarily! This trait
provides both checked and unchecked casting into various kinds of values.

This trait is automatically implemented for any type imported in a
`#[wasm_bindgen]` `extern` block.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasm_bindgen/cast.rs.html#129)#### fn [instanceof](https://docs.rs#tymethod.instanceof)(val: &[JsValue](https://docs.rs/struct.JsValue.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasm_bindgen/cast.rs.html#129)

#### fn [instanceof](https://docs.rs#tymethod.instanceof)(val: &[JsValue](https://docs.rs/struct.JsValue.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Performs a dynamic `instanceof` check to see whether the `JsValue`
provided is an instance of this type.

This is intended to be an internal implementation detail, you likely
won’t need to call this. It’s generally called through the
`is_instance_of` method instead.

instance of `Self`

Performs a zero-cost unchecked conversion from a `&JsValue` into an
instance of `&Self`.

Note the safety of this method, which basically means that `Self` must
be a newtype wrapper around `JsValue`.

This is intended to be an internal implementation detail, you likely won’t need to call this.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Test whether this JS value has a type `T`.

This method will dynamically check to see if this JS object can be
casted to the JS object of type `T`. Usually this uses the `instanceof`
operator. This also works with primitive types like
booleans/strings/numbers as well as cross-realm object like `Array`
which can originate from other iframes.

In general this is intended to be a more robust version of
`is_instance_of`, but if you want strictly the `instanceof` operator
it’s recommended to use that instead.

Performs a dynamic cast (checked at runtime) of this value into the
target type `T`.

This method will return `Err(self)` if `self.has_type::<T>()`
returns `false`, and otherwise it will return `Ok(T)` manufactured with
an unchecked cast (verified correct via the `has_type` operation).

Performs a dynamic cast (checked at runtime) of this value into the
target type `T`.

This method will return `None` if `self.has_type::<T>()`
returns `false`, and otherwise it will return `Some(&T)` manufactured
with an unchecked cast (verified correct via the `has_type` operation).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasm_bindgen/cast.rs.html#82-87)#### fn [unchecked_into](https://docs.rs#method.unchecked_into)<T>(self) -> T

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasm_bindgen/cast.rs.html#82-87)

#### fn [unchecked_into](https://docs.rs#method.unchecked_into)<T>(self) -> T

Performs a zero-cost unchecked cast into the specified type.

This method will convert the `self` value to the type `T`, where both
`self` and `T` are simple wrappers around `JsValue`. This method **does
not check whether  self is an instance of T**. If used incorrectly
then this method may cause runtime exceptions in both Rust and JS, this
should be used with caution.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasm_bindgen/cast.rs.html#100-105)#### fn [unchecked_ref](https://docs.rs#method.unchecked_ref)<T>(&self) -> [&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasm_bindgen/cast.rs.html#100-105)

#### fn [unchecked_ref](https://docs.rs#method.unchecked_ref)<T>(&self) -> [&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)

Performs a zero-cost unchecked cast into a reference to the specified type.

This method will convert the `self` value to the type `T`, where both
`self` and `T` are simple wrappers around `JsValue`. This method **does
not check whether  self is an instance of T**. If used incorrectly
then this method may cause runtime exceptions in both Rust and JS, this
should be used with caution.

This method, unlike `unchecked_into`, does not consume ownership of
`self` and instead works over a shared reference.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasm_bindgen/cast.rs.html#116-121)#### fn [is_instance_of](https://docs.rs#method.is_instance_of)<T>(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasm_bindgen/cast.rs.html#116-121)

#### fn [is_instance_of](https://docs.rs#method.is_instance_of)<T>(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Test whether this JS value is an instance of the type `T`.

This method performs a dynamic check (at runtime) using the JS
`instanceof` operator. This method returns `self instanceof T`.

Note that `instanceof` does not always work with primitive values or
across different realms (e.g. iframes). If you’re not sure whether you
specifically need only `instanceof` it’s recommended to use `has_type`
instead.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasm_bindgen/cast.rs.html#140-142)#### fn [is_type_of](https://docs.rs#method.is_type_of)(val: &[JsValue](https://docs.rs/struct.JsValue.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/wasm_bindgen/cast.rs.html#140-142)

#### fn [is_type_of](https://docs.rs#method.is_type_of)(val: &[JsValue](https://docs.rs/struct.JsValue.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Performs a dynamic check to see whether the `JsValue` provided
is a value of this type.

Unlike `instanceof`, this can be specialised to use a custom check by
adding a `#[wasm_bindgen(is_type_of = callback)]` attribute to the
type import declaration.

Other than that, this is intended to be an internal implementation
detail of `has_type` and you likely won’t need to call this.

# UnwrapThrowExt in wasm_bindgen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/wasm_bindgen/trait.UnwrapThrowExt.html

`pub trait UnwrapThrowExt<T>: `[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [expect_throw](https://docs.rs#tymethod.expect_throw)(self, message: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> T;
    // Provided method
    fn [unwrap_throw](https://docs.rs#method.unwrap_throw)(self) -> T { ... }
}## Expand description

An extension trait for `Option<T>` and `Result<T, E>` for unwrapping the `T`
value, or throwing a JS error if it is not available.

These methods should have a smaller code size footprint than the normal
`Option::unwrap` and `Option::expect` methods, but they are specific to
working with Wasm and JS.

On non-wasm32 targets, defaults to the normal unwrap/expect calls.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use wasm_bindgen::prelude::*;
// If the value is `Option::Some` or `Result::Ok`, then we just get the
// contained `T` value.
let x = Some(42);
assert_eq!(x.unwrap_throw(), 42);
let y: Option<i32> = None;
// This call would throw an error to JS!
//
//     y.unwrap_throw()
//
// And this call would throw an error to JS with a custom error message!
//
//     y.expect_throw("woopsie daisy!")
```
## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# externref_heap_live_count in wasm_bindgen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/wasm_bindgen/fn.externref_heap_live_count.html

`pub fn externref_heap_live_count() -> `[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)## Expand description

Get the count of live `externref`s / `JsValue`s in `wasm-bindgen`’s heap.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

This is intended for debugging and writing tests.

To write a test that asserts against unnecessarily keeping `anref`s /
`JsValue`s alive:

-
get an initial live count,
-
perform some series of operations or function calls that should clean up after themselves, and should not keep holding onto `externref`s /`JsValue`s after completion,
-
get the final live count,
-
and assert that the initial and final counts are the same.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-counted)What is Counted

Note that this only counts the *owned* `externref`s / `JsValue`s that end up in
`wasm-bindgen`’s heap. It does not count borrowed `externref`s / `JsValue`s
that are on its stack.

For example, these `JsValue`s are accounted for:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn my_function(this_is_counted: JsValue) {
    let also_counted = JsValue::from_str("hi");
    assert!(wasm_bindgen::externref_heap_live_count() >= 2);
}
```
While this borrowed `JsValue` ends up on the stack, not the heap, and
therefore is not accounted for:

# intern in wasm_bindgen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/wasm_bindgen/fn.intern.html

## Expand description

Interns Rust strings so that it’s much faster to send them to JS.

Sending strings from Rust to JS is slow, because it has to do a full `O(n)`
copy and *also* encode from UTF-8 to UTF-16. This must be done every single
time a string is sent to JS.

If you are sending the same string multiple times, you can call this `intern`
function, which simply returns its argument unchanged:

`intern("foo") // returns "foo"`However, if you enable the `"enable-interning"` feature for wasm-bindgen,
then it will add the string into an internal cache.

When you send that cached string to JS, it will look it up in the cache,
which completely avoids the `O(n)` copy and encoding. This has a significant
speed boost (as high as 783%)!

However, there is a small cost to this caching, so you shouldn’t cache every string. Only cache strings which have a high likelihood of being sent to JS multiple times.

Also, keep in mind that this function is a *performance hint*: it’s not
*guaranteed* that the string will be cached, and the caching strategy
might change at any time, so don’t rely upon it.

---

# throw_str in wasm_bindgen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/wasm_bindgen/fn.throw_str.html

## Expand description

Throws a JS exception.

This function will throw a JS exception with the message provided. The function will not return as the Wasm stack will be popped when the exception is thrown.

Note that it is very easy to leak memory with this function because this
function, unlike `panic!` on other platforms, **will not run destructors**.
It’s recommended to return a `Result` where possible to avoid the worry of
leaks.

If you need destructors to run, consider using `panic!` when building with
`-Cpanic=unwind`. If the `std` feature is used panics will be caught at the
JavaScript boundary and converted to JavaScript exceptions.

---

# throw_val in wasm_bindgen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/wasm_bindgen/fn.throw_val.html

## Expand description

Rethrow a JS exception

This function will throw a JS exception with the JS value provided. This function will not return and the Wasm stack will be popped until the point of entry of Wasm itself.

Note that it is very easy to leak memory with this function because this
function, unlike `panic!` on other platforms, **will not run destructors**.
It’s recommended to return a `Result` where possible to avoid the worry of
leaks.

If you need destructors to run, consider using `panic!` when building with
`-Cpanic=unwind`. If the `std` feature is used panics will be caught at the
JavaScript boundary and converted to JavaScript exceptions.

---

# wasm_bindgen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/latest/wasm_bindgen/

## Expand description

Runtime support for the `wasm-bindgen` tool

This crate contains the runtime support necessary for `wasm-bindgen` the
attribute and tool. Crates pull in the `#[wasm_bindgen]` attribute through
this crate and this crate also provides JS bindings through the `JsValue`
interface.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

[§](https://docs.rs#enable-interning)`enable-interning`

Enables the internal cache for [`wasm_bindgen::intern`].

This feature currently enables the `std` feature, meaning that it is not
compatible with `no_std` environments.

[§](https://docs.rs#std-default)`std` (default)

Enabling this feature will make the crate depend on the Rust standard library.

Disable this feature to use this crate in `no_std` environments.

[§](https://docs.rs#strict-macro)`strict-macro`

All warnings the `#[wasm_bindgen]` macro emits are turned into hard errors.
This mainly affects unused attribute options.

[§](https://docs.rs#deprecated-features)Deprecated features

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-serialize)`serde-serialize`

**Deprecated:** Use the [ serde-wasm-bindgen](https://docs.rs/serde-wasm-bindgen/latest/serde_wasm_bindgen/) crate instead.

Enables the `JsValue::from_serde` and `JsValue::into_serde` methods for
serializing and deserializing Rust types to and from JavaScript.

[§](https://docs.rs#spans)`spans`

**Deprecated:** This feature became a no-op in wasm-bindgen v0.2.20 (Sep 7, 2018).

# cfg-if

A macro to ergonomically define an item depending on a large number of #[cfg] parameters. Structured like an if-else chain, the first matching branch is the item that gets emitted.

# once_cell 1.21.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/once_cell/^1.12

# Overview

`once_cell` provides two new cell-like types, `unsync::OnceCell` and `sync::OnceCell`. `OnceCell`
might store arbitrary non-`Copy` types, can be assigned to at most once and provide direct access
to the stored contents. In a nutshell, API looks *roughly* like this:

```
```
Note that, like with `RefCell` and `Mutex`, the `set` method requires only a shared reference.
Because of the single assignment restriction `get` can return an `&T` instead of `Ref<T>`
or `MutexGuard<T>`.

`once_cell` also has a `Lazy<T>` type, build on top of `OnceCell` which provides the same API as
the `lazy_static!` macro, but without using any macros:

```
use ;
use Lazy;
static GLOBAL_DATA:  = new;
```
More patterns and use-cases are in the [docs](https://docs.rs/once_cell/)!

# serde_json 1.0.150 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/serde_json/^1.0

**Serde is a framework for  serializing and deserializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.**

```
[]
 = "1.0"
```
You may be looking for:

- [JSON API documentation](https://docs.rs/serde_json)
- [Serde API documentation](https://docs.rs/serde)
- [Detailed documentation about Serde](https://serde.rs/)
- [Setting up](https://serde.rs/derive.html)- `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]`
- [Release notes](https://github.com/serde-rs/json/releases)

JSON is a ubiquitous open-standard format that uses human-readable text to transmit data objects consisting of key-value pairs.

```
```
There are three common ways that you might find yourself needing to work with JSON data in Rust.

- **As text data.**An unprocessed string of JSON data that you receive on an HTTP endpoint, read from a file, or prepare to send to a remote server.
- **As an untyped or loosely typed representation.**Maybe you want to check that some JSON data is valid before passing it on, but without knowing the structure of what it contains. Or you want to do very basic manipulations like insert a key in a particular spot.
- **As a strongly typed Rust data structure.**When you expect all or most of your data to conform to a particular structure and want to get real work done without JSON's loosey-goosey nature tripping you up.

Serde JSON provides efficient, flexible, safe ways of converting data between each of these representations.

## Operating on untyped JSON values

Any valid JSON data can be manipulated in the following recursive enum
representation. This data structure is [ serde_json::Value](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/value/enum.Value.html).

```
```
A string of JSON data can be parsed into a `serde_json::Value` by the
[ serde_json::from_str](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/de/fn.from_str.html) function. There is also

[for parsing from a byte slice](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/de/fn.from_slice.html)

`from_slice``&[u8]` and
[for parsing from any](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/de/fn.from_reader.html)

`from_reader``io::Read` like a File or a
TCP stream.```
use ;
```
The result of square bracket indexing like `v["name"]` is a borrow of the data
at that index, so the type is `&Value`. A JSON map can be indexed with string
keys, while a JSON array can be indexed with integer keys. If the type of the
data is not right for the type with which it is being indexed, or if a map does
not contain the key being indexed, or if the index into a vector is out of
bounds, the returned element is `Value::Null`.

When a `Value` is printed, it is printed as a JSON string. So in the code above,
the output looks like `Please call "John Doe" at the number "+44 1234567"`. The
quotation marks appear because `v["name"]` is a `&Value` containing a JSON
string and its JSON representation is `"John Doe"`. Printing as a plain string
without quotation marks involves converting from a JSON string to a Rust string
with [ as_str()](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/enum.Value.html#method.as_str) or avoiding the use of

`Value` as described in the following
section.The `Value` representation is sufficient for very basic tasks but can be tedious
to work with for anything more significant. Error handling is verbose to
implement correctly, for example imagine trying to detect the presence of
unrecognized fields in the input data. The compiler is powerless to help you
when you make a mistake, for example imagine typoing `v["name"]` as `v["nmae"]`
in one of the dozens of places it is used in your code.

## Parsing JSON as strongly typed data structures

Serde provides a powerful way of mapping JSON data into Rust data structures largely automatically.

```
use ;
use Result;
```
This is the same `serde_json::from_str` function as before, but this time we
assign the return value to a variable of type `Person` so Serde will
automatically interpret the input data as a `Person` and produce informative
error messages if the layout does not conform to what a `Person` is expected to
look like.

Any type that implements Serde's `Deserialize` trait can be deserialized this
way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>` and
`HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Deserialize)]`.

Once we have `p` of type `Person`, our IDE and the Rust compiler can help us use
it correctly like they do for any other Rust code. The IDE can autocomplete
field names to prevent typos, which was impossible in the `serde_json::Value`
representation. And the Rust compiler can check that when we write
`p.phones[0]`, then `p.phones` is guaranteed to be a `Vec<String>` so indexing
into it makes sense and produces a `String`.

The necessary setup for using Serde's derive macros is explained on the * Using
derive* page of the Serde site.

## Constructing JSON values

Serde JSON provides a [ json! macro](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/macro.json.html) to build

`serde_json::Value`
objects with very natural JSON syntax.```
use json;
```
The `Value::to_string()` function converts a `serde_json::Value` into a `String`
of JSON text.

One neat thing about the `json!` macro is that variables and expressions can be
interpolated directly into the JSON value as you are building it. Serde will
check at compile time that the value you are interpolating is able to be
represented as JSON.

```
let full_name = "John Doe";
let age_last_year = 42;
// The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
let john = json!;
```
This is amazingly convenient, but we have the problem we had before with
`Value`: the IDE and Rust compiler cannot help us if we get it wrong. Serde JSON
provides a better way of serializing strongly-typed data structures into JSON
text.

## Creating JSON by serializing data structures

A data structure can be converted to a JSON string by
[ serde_json::to_string](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/ser/fn.to_string.html). There is also

[which serializes to a](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/ser/fn.to_vec.html)

`serde_json::to_vec``Vec<u8>` and
[which serializes to any](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/ser/fn.to_writer.html)

`serde_json::to_writer``io::Write`
such as a File or a TCP stream.```
use ;
use Result;
```
Any type that implements Serde's `Serialize` trait can be serialized this way.
This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>` and `HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with `#[derive(Serialize)]`.

## Performance

It is fast. You should expect in the ballpark of 500 to 1000 megabytes per
second deserialization and 600 to 900 megabytes per second serialization,
depending on the characteristics of your data. This is competitive with the
fastest C and C++ JSON libraries or even 30% faster for many use cases.
Benchmarks live in the [serde-rs/json-benchmark](https://github.com/serde-rs/json-benchmark) repo.

## Getting help

Serde is one of the most widely used Rust libraries, so any place that
Rustaceans congregate will be able to help you out. For chat, consider trying
the [#rust-questions](https://discord.com/channels/273534239310479360/274215136414400513) or [#rust-beginners](https://discord.com/channels/273534239310479360/273541522815713281) channels of the unofficial community
Discord (invite: [https://discord.gg/rust-lang-community](https://discord.gg/rust-lang-community)), the [#rust-usage](https://discord.com/channels/442252698964721669/443150878111694848) or
[#beginners](https://discord.com/channels/442252698964721669/448238009733742612) channels of the official Rust Project Discord (invite:
[https://discord.gg/rust-lang](https://discord.gg/rust-lang)), or the [#general](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/122651-general) stream in Zulip. For
asynchronous, consider the [[rust] tag on StackOverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/rust), the
[/r/rust](https://www.reddit.com/r/rust) subreddit which has a pinned weekly easy questions post, or the Rust
[Discourse forum](https://users.rust-lang.org). It's acceptable to file a support issue in this
repo, but they tend not to get as many eyes as any of the above and may get
closed without a response after some time.

## No-std support

As long as there is a memory allocator, it is possible to use serde_json without the rest of the Rust standard library. Disable the default "std" feature and enable the "alloc" feature:

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0",  = false,  = ["alloc"] }
```
For JSON support in Serde without a memory allocator, please see the
[ serde-json-core](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/serde-json-core) crate.

# wasm-bindgen-macro 0.2.126 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wasm-bindgen-macro/=0.2.126

`wasm-bindgen-macro`

Implementation of the `#[wasm_bindgen]` attribute. See the `wasm-bindgen`
documentation for more information about what this macro does.

## Testing

Testing of this macro is done through "ui tests" in the `ui-tests` subdirectory
of this crate. Each Rust file in this folder is compiled with the `wasm_bindgen`
crate, and the `*.stderr` file sitting next to it is the asserted output of the
compiler. If the output matches, the test passes, and if the output doesn't
match the test fails. Note that it is also considered a failure if a test
actually compiles successfully.

To add a test:

-
Create `ui-tests/my-awesome-test.rs`
-
Write an invalid `#[wasm_bindgen]`invocation, testing the error you're generating
-
Execute `cargo test -p wasm-bindgen-macro --test ui`, the test will fail
-
From within the `ui-tests`folder, execute`./update-all-references.sh`. This should create a`my-awesome-test.stderr`file.OR if you are on Windows, set the `TRYBUILD=overwrite`environment variable (this is done as`$env:TRYBUILD="overwrite"`[in powershell](https://stackoverflow.com/a/1333717/7595472)) and run the command again.
-
Inspect `my-awesome-test.stderr`to make sure it looks ok
-
Rerun `cargo test -p wasm-bindgen-macro --test ui`and your tests should pass!

# once_cell 1.21.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/once_cell/^1

# Overview

`once_cell` provides two new cell-like types, `unsync::OnceCell` and `sync::OnceCell`. `OnceCell`
might store arbitrary non-`Copy` types, can be assigned to at most once and provide direct access
to the stored contents. In a nutshell, API looks *roughly* like this:

```
```
Note that, like with `RefCell` and `Mutex`, the `set` method requires only a shared reference.
Because of the single assignment restriction `get` can return an `&T` instead of `Ref<T>`
or `MutexGuard<T>`.

`once_cell` also has a `Lazy<T>` type, build on top of `OnceCell` which provides the same API as
the `lazy_static!` macro, but without using any macros:

```
use ;
use Lazy;
static GLOBAL_DATA:  = new;
```
More patterns and use-cases are in the [docs](https://docs.rs/once_cell/)!

# rustversion 1.0.22 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rustversion/^1.0.6

# Compiler version cfg

This crate provides macros for conditional compilation according to rustc
compiler version, analogous to [ #[cfg(...)]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg-attribute) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg_attr-attribute)

`#[cfg_attr(...)]````
[]
 = "1.0"
```
## Selectors

-
`#[rustversion::stable]`— True on any stable compiler.
-
`#[rustversion::stable(1.34)]`— True on exactly the specified stable compiler.
-
`#[rustversion::beta]`— True on any beta compiler.
-
`#[rustversion::nightly]`— True on any nightly compiler or dev build.
-
`#[rustversion::nightly(2025-01-01)]`— True on exactly one nightly.
-
`#[rustversion::since(1.34)]`— True on that stable release and any later compiler, including beta and nightly.
-
`#[rustversion::since(2025-01-01)]`— True on that nightly and all newer ones.
-
`#[rustversion::before(`version or date`)]`— Negative of*#[rustversion::since(...)]*.
-
`#[rustversion::not(`selector`)]`— Negative of any selector; for example*#[rustversion::not(nightly)]*.
-
`#[rustversion::any(`selectors...`)]`— True if any of the comma-separated selectors is true; for example*#[rustversion::any(stable, beta)]*.
-
`#[rustversion::all(`selectors...`)]`— True if all of the comma-separated selectors are true; for example*#[rustversion::all(since(1.31), before(1.34))]*.
-
`#[rustversion::attr(`selector`,`attribute`)]`— For conditional inclusion of attributes; analogous to`cfg_attr`.
-
`rustversion::cfg!(`selector`)`— An expression form of any of the above attributes; for example*if rustversion::cfg!(any(stable, beta)) { ... }*.

## Use cases

Providing additional trait impls as types are stabilized in the standard library
without breaking compatibility with older compilers; in this case Pin<P>
stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2019/02/28/Rust-1.33.0.html#pinning):

```
use Pin;
```
Similar but for language features; the ability to control alignment greater than
1 of packed structs was stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/RELEASES.md#version-1330-2019-02-28).

```
;
```
Augmenting code with `const` as const impls are stabilized in the standard
library. This use of `const` as an attribute is recognized as a special case by
the rustversion::attr macro.

```
use Duration;
```
Emitting Cargo cfg directives from a build script. Note that this requires
listing `rustversion` under `[build-dependencies]` in Cargo.toml, not
`[dependencies]`.

```
// build.rs
```
```
// src/lib.rs
extern crate alloc;
```

# paste 1.0.15 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/paste/^1

# Macros for all your token pasting needs

The nightly-only [ concat_idents!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/macro.concat_idents.html) macro in the Rust standard library is
notoriously underpowered in that its concatenated identifiers can only refer to
existing items, they can never be used to define something new.

This crate provides a flexible way to paste together identifiers in a macro, including using pasted identifiers to define new items.

```
[]
 = "1.0"
```
This approach works with any Rust compiler 1.31+.

## Pasting identifiers

Within the `paste!` macro, identifiers inside `[<`...`>]` are pasted together to
form a single identifier.

```
use paste;
paste!
```
## More elaborate example

The next example shows a macro that generates accessor methods for some struct fields. It demonstrates how you might find it useful to bundle a paste invocation inside of a macro_rules macro.

```
use paste;
    }
}
make_a_struct_and_getters!;
```
## Case conversion

Use `$var:lower` or `$var:upper` in the segment list to convert an interpolated
segment to lower- or uppercase as part of the paste. For example, `[<ld_ $reg:lower _expr>]` would paste to `ld_bc_expr` if invoked with $reg=`Bc`.

Use `$var:snake` to convert CamelCase input to snake_case.
Use `$var:camel` to convert snake_case to CamelCase.
These compose, so for example `$var:snake:upper` would give you SCREAMING_CASE.

The precise Unicode conversions are as defined by [ str::to_lowercase](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.to_lowercase) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.to_uppercase)

`str::to_uppercase`## Pasting documentation strings

Within the `paste!` macro, arguments to a #[doc ...] attribute are implicitly
concatenated together to form a coherent documentation string.

```
use paste;
method_new!;  // expands to #[doc = "Create a new `Paste` object"]
```

# wasm-bindgen 0.2.125 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wasm-bindgen/0.2.125

Built with 🦀🕸 by The Rust and WebAssembly Working Group

## Install `wasm-bindgen-cli`

You can install it using `cargo install`:

```
cargo install wasm-bindgen-cli
```
Or, you can download it from the
[release page](https://github.com/wasm-bindgen/wasm-bindgen/releases).

If you have [ cargo-binstall](https://crates.io/crates/cargo-binstall) installed,
then you can install the pre-built artifacts by running:

```
cargo binstall wasm-bindgen-cli
```
## Example

Import JavaScript things into Rust and export Rust things to JavaScript.

```
use *;
// Import the `window.alert` function from the Web.
extern "C"
// Export a `greet` function from Rust to JavaScript, that alerts a
// hello message.
```
Use exported Rust things from JavaScript with ECMAScript modules!

```
import  from "./hello_world";
;
```
## Features

-
**Lightweight.**Only pay for what you use.`wasm-bindgen`only generates bindings and glue for the JavaScript imports you actually use and Rust functionality that you export. For example, importing and using the`document.querySelector`method doesn't cause`Node.prototype.appendChild`or`window.alert`to be included in the bindings as well.
-
**ECMAScript modules.**Just import WebAssembly modules the same way you would import JavaScript modules. Future compatible with[WebAssembly modules and ECMAScript modules integration](https://github.com/WebAssembly/esm-integration).
-
**Designed with the**Eventually, there won't be any JavaScript shims between Rust-generated wasm functions and native DOM methods. Because the Wasm functions are statically type checked, some of those native methods' dynamic type checks should become unnecessary, promising to unlock even-faster-than-JavaScript DOM access.["Web IDL bindings" proposal](https://github.com/WebAssembly/proposals/issues/8)in mind.

## Guide

## API Docs

## MSRV Policy

- Libraries that are released on [crates.io](https://crates.io)have a MSRV of v1.77.
- CLI tools and their corresponding support libraries have a MSRV of v1.86.

The project aims to maintain a 2-year MSRV policy for libraries (meaning we support Rust versions released within the last 2 years), but with a shorter MSRV policy for the CLI. Changes to the MSRV may be made in patch versions, and will be logged in the CHANGELOG and MSRV history below.

### MSRV History

| Version | Library MSRV | CLI MSRV | Date |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.2.118 | 1.77 | 1.86 | 2026-04-10 |
| 0.2.106 | 1.71 | 1.82 | 2025-11-27 |
| 0.2.103 | 1.57 | 1.82 | 2025-09-17 |
| 0.2.93 | 1.57 | 1.76 | 2024-08-13 |

- Libraries that are released on [crates.io](https://crates.io)have a MSRV of v1.71.
- CLI tools and their corresponding support libraries have a MSRV of v1.82.

The project aims to maintain a 2-year MSRV policy for libraries (meaning we support Rust versions released within the last 2 years), but with a shorter MSRV policy for the CLI. Changes to the MSRV may be made in patch versions, and will be logged in the CHANGELOG and MSRV history below.

### MSRV History

| Version | Library MSRV | CLI MSRV | Date |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.2.106 | 1.71 | 1.82 | 2025-11-xx |
| 0.2.103 | 1.57 | 1.82 | 2025-09-17 |
| 0.2.93 | 1.57 | 1.76 | 2024-08-13 |

# wasm-bindgen 0.2.113 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wasm-bindgen/0.2.113

Built with 🦀🕸 by The Rust and WebAssembly Working Group

## Install `wasm-bindgen-cli`

You can install it using `cargo install`:

```
cargo install wasm-bindgen-cli
```
Or, you can download it from the
[release page](https://github.com/wasm-bindgen/wasm-bindgen/releases).

If you have [ cargo-binstall](https://crates.io/crates/cargo-binstall) installed,
then you can install the pre-built artifacts by running:

```
cargo binstall wasm-bindgen-cli
```
## Example

Import JavaScript things into Rust and export Rust things to JavaScript.

```
use *;
// Import the `window.alert` function from the Web.
extern "C"
// Export a `greet` function from Rust to JavaScript, that alerts a
// hello message.
```
Use exported Rust things from JavaScript with ECMAScript modules!

```
import  from "./hello_world";
;
```
## Features

-
**Lightweight.**Only pay for what you use.`wasm-bindgen`only generates bindings and glue for the JavaScript imports you actually use and Rust functionality that you export. For example, importing and using the`document.querySelector`method doesn't cause`Node.prototype.appendChild`or`window.alert`to be included in the bindings as well.
-
**ECMAScript modules.**Just import WebAssembly modules the same way you would import JavaScript modules. Future compatible with[WebAssembly modules and ECMAScript modules integration](https://github.com/WebAssembly/esm-integration).
-
**Designed with the**Eventually, there won't be any JavaScript shims between Rust-generated wasm functions and native DOM methods. Because the Wasm functions are statically type checked, some of those native methods' dynamic type checks should become unnecessary, promising to unlock even-faster-than-JavaScript DOM access.["Web IDL bindings" proposal](https://github.com/WebAssembly/proposals/issues/8)in mind.

## Guide

## API Docs

## MSRV Policy

- Libraries that are released on [crates.io](https://crates.io)have a MSRV of v1.71.
- CLI tools and their corresponding support libraries have a MSRV of v1.82.

The project aims to maintain a 2-year MSRV policy for libraries (meaning we support Rust versions released within the last 2 years), but with a shorter MSRV policy for the CLI. Changes to the MSRV may be made in patch versions, and will be logged in the CHANGELOG and MSRV history below.

### MSRV History

| Version | Library MSRV | CLI MSRV | Date |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.2.106 | 1.71 | 1.82 | 2025-11-xx |
| 0.2.103 | 1.57 | 1.82 | 2025-09-17 |
| 0.2.93 | 1.57 | 1.76 | 2024-08-13 |

## License

- Apache License, Version 2.0, ([LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE)or[http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0))

at your option.
